background:
Research question: How do domestic spaces and everyday caregiving shape preschool children's physical activity? The study explores parents' and grandparents' perceptions of young children's activities inside and outside the home, and asks whether lived experiences of caregiving fit current physical activity policy.
Site and participants: Lower-income families in Eugene and the Springfield metropolitan area, Oregon, USA. There were 16 families, each with a child aged 3–5 years and at least one grandparent who cared for the child at least twice a month. Participants were 22 parents and 27 grandparents.
How the data were collected: The Grandparents Study (2011) carried out semi-structured interviews with 49 parents and grandparents. They were recruited through Craigslist and local newspaper adverts. PN and a research assistant interviewed each person separately for 1.5–2.5 hours; interviews were videotaped and transcribed. Participants also filled in socio-demographic questionnaires, and the children were weighed and measured.
Coding task (the same for every excerpt set): open and axial coding; selective coding only as a tentative core
This section of the study: How families handle young children's vigorous play inside the home when the weather, space limits or household rules keep children from playing outdoors.
Concepts the study works with: materialities of care; spatialities of care; mundane movement

How the data were collected: A scientometric analysis of 18 WoS-indexed STS journals. Coding task (the same for every excerpt set): open and axial coding; selective coding only as a tentative core

Concepts the study works with: typification; doability; formulaic writing; projectification

background:
Research question: How internalised ableism shows up as a health and wellbeing issue for disabled young people, with psychological, social and physical consequences, and how solidarity and peer support may help them heal from it.
Site and participants: Disabled young people in Iceland: ten men and eleven women, aged 18–35, with mobility, sensory, intellectual and psychosocial impairments. About 80% had been disabled since birth. All identified as disabled.
How the data were collected: Four focus-group interviews, held from spring 2018 to autumn 2019 as part of a larger project. Each lasted 1.5–2 hours and was moderated by two researchers who identify as disabled. Two groups were mixed, one was women only and one men only. Participants talked about their childhood, wellbeing, and what helps or threatens it. Sessions were recorded and transcribed verbatim.
Coding task (the same for every excerpt set): open and axial coding; selective coding only as a tentative core
This section of the study: Mental health, romantic relationships, expectations placed on disabled children, and childhood freedom, looked at in terms of how ableism shapes self-worth.
Concepts the study works with: internalised ableism; core shame identity; shame

Research question: How do women with HIV see HIV/AIDS compared with other traumatic events in their lives? Is HIV the most disruptive event? What separates women for whom it is most disruptive from those for whom it is not? How do they reconstruct HIV's meaning in their life stories?
Site and participants: 37 women with HIV infection living mostly in the Northeastern United States. They were aged 27–60 and mostly white, with some black and Latina women. Most had drug use histories, were well linked to services and were in good functional health. Five had an AIDS diagnosis.

This section of the study: Intimate partner violence and abuse in the lives of women with HIV, and how they weigh these experiences against living with the infection.

Research question: How do rural communities in Montes de María relate to and experience the state while the 2016 peace accords are put into practice? The study looks at the participatory process that produced the territorially focused development plans (PDET) and how they were first implemented. It asks how state abandonment and territorial citizenship shape access to rights.
Site and participants: Campesino communities in Montes de María, a sub-region of fifteen municipalities that was badly affected by the armed conflict and is one of the PDET territories. The fieldwork centred on the rural area of the municipality of Ovejas. Officials of the Territorial Renewal Agency (ART) and NGOs were also part of the study.
How the data were collected: Twelve months of ethnographic fieldwork (September 2017 to August 2018), followed by three one-month visits in 2019, 2021 and 2022. The author did participant observation in campesino daily life and organisations, and in veredal, community and municipal PDET assemblies. There were forty semi-structured interviews with campesinos, plus further interviews with the regional ART team and NGOs.
Coding task (the same for every excerpt set): open and axial coding; selective coding only as a tentative core

background:
Research question: How do professionals in English critical care account for the changes associated with public-sector 'modernisation'? In what ways have they used modernisation as a strategy for professional gain, and why might their accounts be more optimistic than those reported from other settings?
Site and participants: Critical care (intensive care) staff in seven hospitals within three critical care networks in England. The hospitals were teaching and general hospitals, rated as more or less 'enthusiastic' modernisers. Staff included doctors, nurses (including outreach nurses), allied health professionals and administrators.
How the data were collected: One author carried out in-depth, audio-recorded interviews with 45 individuals: 11 medical, 20 nursing, 12 allied health and 2 administrators. The interviews took place between April 2007 and February 2008, within a larger evaluation of the modernisation programme. A topic guide covered work histories, change over time and specific modernisation activities. Long-serving staff were purposively sampled.
Coding task (the same for every excerpt set): open and axial coding; selective coding only as a tentative core
This section of the study: How critical care staff (doctors, nurses and allied health professionals) describe changes in their status, authority, autonomy and working relationships within the hospital since modernisation.
Concepts the study works with: Modernisation; professionalising strategy; professionalising project; professional autonomy; new professionalism

background:
Research question: What distinct forms of wage theft occur in hospitality, and how do employers' practices lead to the theft of employees' wages? The study treats wage theft as the extraction of additional unpaid labour time, part of capitalism as a system and not only a breach of the law.
Site and participants: Hotel workers in London: 16 hotels and six staffing agencies. Participants included workers employed by hotels and agency workers in many jobs (chefs, room attendants, waiters, doormen, supervisors), plus some managers and a union organiser.
How the data were collected: The first author did participant observation in 2016, working through three temporary work agencies and attending union meetings and surgeries. This came to about 150 hours over six months. There were also 35 semi-structured interviews of 45–90 minutes: 30 with workers (21 hotel, nine agency) and five with managers. Company documents were also used.
Coding task (the same for every excerpt set): open and axial coding; selective coding only as a tentative core
This section of the study: Working time in hotel work: how hours on the job are counted, set and paid for chefs, housekeeping staff and agency workers.
Concepts the study works with: wage theft; additional unpaid labour time; theft of labour time; rate of exploitation; Method of Extraction; Absolute surplus-value

background:
Research question: How do clinicians in specialist autism teams use and interpret evidence together in post-assessment meetings to build an accountable diagnostic narrative? The authors also ask how this joint diagnostic work might help make autism into a fixed condition (reification).
Site and participants: Four National Health Service specialist autism assessment teams in the south of England: two adult teams and two children and young people teams. Members included psychiatrists, clinical psychologists, assistant psychologists, speech and language therapists, managers and others. Patients and families were not present at the meetings.
How the data were collected: The first author observed and audio-recorded 18 team meetings: nine at the two adult teams and nine at the two children's teams. The meetings covered 88 cases over more than 19 hours. 51 cases were analysed (24 children and young people, 27 adults). The data also included field notes and short case summaries. The study period is not stated.
Coding task (the same for every excerpt set): open and axial coding; selective coding only as a tentative core
This section of the study: How clinicians in diagnostic meetings draw on, weigh and judge the credibility of accounts of behaviour given by patients, parents and friends who are not present.
Concepts the study works with: narrate objectivity; disciplinary objectivity; space between fields; credit‐worthiness; reification

background:
Research question: How do domestic spaces and everyday caregiving shape preschool children's physical activity? The study explores parents' and grandparents' perceptions of young children's activities inside and outside the home, and asks whether lived experiences of caregiving fit current physical activity policy.
Site and participants: Lower-income families in Eugene and the Springfield metropolitan area, Oregon, USA. There were 16 families, each with a child aged 3–5 years and at least one grandparent who cared for the child at least twice a month. Participants were 22 parents and 27 grandparents.
How the data were collected: The Grandparents Study (2011) carried out semi-structured interviews with 49 parents and grandparents. They were recruited through Craigslist and local newspaper adverts. PN and a research assistant interviewed each person separately for 1.5–2.5 hours; interviews were videotaped and transcribed. Participants also filled in socio-demographic questionnaires, and the children were weighed and measured.
Coding task (the same for every excerpt set): open and axial coding; selective coding only as a tentative core
This section of the study: How families handle young children's vigorous play inside the home when the weather, space limits or household rules keep children from playing outdoors.
Concepts the study works with: materialities of care; spatialities of care; mundane movement
